claim: HNF4α has been implicated in colitis and colon cancer in humans.
source: HNF4α has been implicated in colitis and colon cancer in humans but the role of the different HNF4α isoforms expressed from the two different promoters (P1 and P2) active in the colon is not clear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Ahn et al., 2008; Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Barrett et al., 2009).

claim: P1-HNF4α is expressed primarily in the differentiated compartment of the mouse colonic crypt.
source: Here, we show that P1-HNF4α is expressed primarily in the differentiated compartment of the mouse colonic crypt and P2-HNF4α in the proliferative compartment.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B-D demonstrating P1-HNF4α localization in the differentiated compartment.

claim: P2-HNF4α is expressed in the proliferative compartment of the mouse colonic crypt.
source: Here, we show that P1-HNF4α is expressed primarily in the differentiated compartment of the mouse colonic crypt and P2-HNF4α in the proliferative compartment.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B-D demonstrating P2-HNF4α localization in the proliferative compartment and co-localization with Ki67.

claim: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different colonic gene expression profiles.
source: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different colonic gene expression profiles, interacting proteins, cellular migration, ion transport and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing differential gene expression between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different interacting proteins.
source: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different colonic gene expression profiles, interacting proteins, cellular migration, ion transport and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: Supported by RIME analysis shown in Figure 5C demonstrating differential protein interactions between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different cellular migration.
source: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different colonic gene expression profiles, interacting proteins, cellular migration, ion transport and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 5D demonstrating differential cell migration between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different ion transport.
source: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different colonic gene expression profiles, interacting proteins, cellular migration, ion transport and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: Supported by Ussing chamber assays shown in Figure 5E demonstrating differential chloride secretion between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different epithelial barrier function.
source: Exon swap mice that express only P1- or only P2-HNF4α have different colonic gene expression profiles, interacting proteins, cellular migration, ion transport and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: Supported by FITC-dextran permeability assays shown in Figure 7C demonstrating differential barrier function between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: The exon swap mice exhibit altered susceptibilities to experimental colitis (DSS).
source: The mice also exhibit altered susceptibilities to experimental colitis (DSS) and colitis-associated colon cancer (AOM+DSS).
evidence: Supported by DSS treatment experiments shown in Figure 4 demonstrating differential mortality, body weight loss, and histological scores between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: The exon swap mice exhibit altered susceptibilities to colitis-associated colon cancer (AOM+DSS).
source: The mice also exhibit altered susceptibilities to experimental colitis (DSS) and colitis-associated colon cancer (AOM+DSS).
evidence: Supported by AOM+DSS treatment experiments shown in Figure 3 demonstrating differential tumor burden between α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice.

claim: P2-HNF4α-only mice have elevated levels of the cytokine resistin-like β (RELMβ).
source: When P2-HNF4α-only mice (which have elevated levels of the cytokine resistin-like β, RELMβ, and are extremely sensitive to DSS) are crossed with Retnlb-/- mice, they are rescued from mortality.
evidence: Supported by microarray and ELISA data shown in Figure 5F demonstrating elevated RELMβ expression in α7HMZ mice.

claim: P2-HNF4α-only mice are extremely sensitive to DSS.
source: When P2-HNF4α-only mice (which have elevated levels of the cytokine resistin-like β, RELMβ, and are extremely sensitive to DSS) are crossed with Retnlb-/- mice, they are rescued from mortality.
evidence: Supported by DSS treatment experiments shown in Figure 4A demonstrating ~73% mortality rate in α7HMZ mice.

claim: When P2-HNF4α-only mice are crossed with Retnlb-/- mice, they are rescued from mortality.
source: When P2-HNF4α-only mice (which have elevated levels of the cytokine resistin-like β, RELMβ, and are extremely sensitive to DSS) are crossed with Retnlb-/- mice, they are rescued from mortality.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 6E demonstrating that RbKO/α7HMZ mice have significantly reduced mortality compared to WT/α7HMZ mice.

claim: P2-HNF4α binds the RELMβ promoter.
source: Furthermore, P2-HNF4α binds and preferentially activates the RELMβ promoter.
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating HNF4α binding to the RETNLB promoter in Caco2 cells.

claim: P2-HNF4α preferentially activates the RELMβ promoter.
source: Furthermore, P2-HNF4α binds and preferentially activates the RELMβ promoter.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assays shown in Figure 7B demonstrating that P2-HNF4α activates the RELMβ promoter significantly more than P1-HNF4α.

claim: HNF4α isoforms perform non-redundant functions in the colon under conditions of stress.
source: In summary, HNF4α isoforms perform non-redundant functions in the colon under conditions of stress, underscoring the importance of tracking them both in colitis and colon cancer.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the differential responses of α1HMZ and α7HMZ mice to DSS and AOM+DSS treatments shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: HNF4α is a highly conserved member of nuclear receptor superfamily of ligand-dependent transcription factors.
source: Hepatocyte nuclear factor 4alpha (HNF4α) (NR2Α1) is a highly conserved member of nuclear receptor superfamily of ligand-dependent transcription factors that is expressed in liver, kidney, pancreas, stomach and intestine (Sladek et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by citation to Sladek et al., 1990.

claim: HNF4α is expressed in liver, kidney, pancreas, stomach and intestine.
source: Hepatocyte nuclear factor 4alpha (HNF4α) (NR2Α1) is a highly conserved member of nuclear receptor superfamily of ligand-dependent transcription factors that is expressed in liver, kidney, pancreas, stomach and intestine (Sladek et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sladek et al., 1990.

claim: HNF4α is a master regulator of liver-specific gene expression.
source: HNF4α is best known for its role in the liver where it is a master regulator of liver-specific gene expression and essential for adult and fetal liver function (Hayhurst et al., 2001; Kaestner, 2010; Bolotin et al., 2010; Odom, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Hayhurst et al., 2001; Kaestner, 2010; Bolotin et al., 2010; Odom, 2004).

claim: HNF4α is essential for adult and fetal liver function.
source: HNF4α is best known for its role in the liver where it is a master regulator of liver-specific gene expression and essential for adult and fetal liver function (Hayhurst et al., 2001; Kaestner, 2010; Bolotin et al., 2010; Odom, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Hayhurst et al., 2001; Kaestner, 2010; Bolotin et al., 2010; Odom, 2004).

claim: HNF4α regulates insulin secretion from beta cells in the pancreas.
source: HNF4α is also known for its role in the pancreas where it regulates insulin secretion from beta cells (Gupta et al., 2007; 2005; Miura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Gupta et al., 2007; 2005; Miura et al., 2006).

claim: Mutations in the HNF4Α gene and promoter regions are associated with Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young 1 (MODY1).
source: Mutations in the HNF4Α gene and promoter regions are associated with Maturity Onset Diabetes of the Young 1 (MODY1) (Ellard and Colclough, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ellard and Colclough, 2006.

claim: Knockout of the Hnf4a gene in the embryonic mouse colon results in disrupted crypt topology.
source: Knockout of the Hnf4a gene in the embryonic mouse colon results in disrupted crypt topology, and a decreased number of epithelial and mature goblet cells (Garrison et al., 2006), while the adult intestinal knockout shows defects in the balance between proliferation and differentiation as well as immune function, ion transport, epithelial barrier function and oxidative stress (Ahn et al., 2008; Cattin et al., 2009; Darsigny et al., 2009; 2010; Chahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garrison et al., 2006.

claim: Knockout of the Hnf4a gene in the embryonic mouse colon results in a decreased number of epithelial and mature goblet cells.
source: Knockout of the Hnf4a gene in the embryonic mouse colon results in disrupted crypt topology, and a decreased number of epithelial and mature goblet cells (Garrison et al., 2006), while the adult intestinal knockout shows defects in the balance between proliferation and differentiation as well as immune function, ion transport, epithelial barrier function and oxidative stress (Ahn et al., 2008; Cattin et al., 2009; Darsigny et al., 2009; 2010; Chahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garrison et al., 2006.

claim: The adult intestinal knockout of Hnf4a shows defects in the balance between proliferation and differentiation.
source: Knockout of the Hnf4a gene in the embryonic mouse colon results in disrupted crypt topology, and a decreased number of epithelial and mature goblet cells (Garrison et al., 2006), while the adult intestinal knockout shows defects in the balance between proliferation and differentiation as well as immune function, ion transport, epithelial barrier function and oxidative stress (Ahn et al., 2008; Cattin et al., 2009; Darsigny et al., 2009; 2010; Chahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Cattin et al., 2009; Darsigny et al., 2009; 2010; Chahar et al., 2014).

claim: The adult intestinal knockout of Hnf4a shows defects in immune function, ion transport, epithelial barrier function and oxidative stress.
source: Knockout of the Hnf4a gene in the embryonic mouse colon results in disrupted crypt topology, and a decreased number of epithelial and mature goblet cells (Garrison et al., 2006), while the adult intestinal knockout shows defects in the balance between proliferation and differentiation as well as immune function, ion transport, epithelial barrier function and oxidative stress (Ahn et al., 2008; Cattin et al., 2009; Darsigny et al., 2009; 2010; Chahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Cattin et al., 2009; Darsigny et al., 2009; 2010; Chahar et al., 2014).

claim: Dysregulation of the HNF4A gene is linked to several gastrointestinal disorders including colitis and colon cancer.
source: Dysregulation of the HNF4A gene is linked to several gastrointestinal disorders including colitis and colon cancer and a single nucleotide polymorphism in the HNF4A gene region is associated with ulcerative colitis (Ahn et al., 2008; Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Barrett et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Barrett et al., 2009).

claim: A single nucleotide polymorphism in the HNF4A gene region is associated with ulcerative colitis.
source: Dysregulation of the HNF4A gene is linked to several gastrointestinal disorders including colitis and colon cancer and a single nucleotide polymorphism in the HNF4A gene region is associated with ulcerative colitis (Ahn et al., 2008; Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Barrett et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006; Oshima et al., 2007; Barrett et al., 2009).

claim: There are two different promoters (proximal P1 and distal P2) in the HNF4α gene that are both active in the colon.
source: There are two different promoters (proximal P1 and distal P2) in the HNF4α gene that are both active in the colon.
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and citations in the text.

claim: The HNF4α promoters are conserved from frog to human.
source: The promoters are conserved from frog to human and, along with alternative splicing, give rise to nine different transcript variants of HNF4α (Huang et al., 2009) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2009.

claim: The HNF4α promoters, along with alternative splicing, give rise to nine different transcript variants of HNF4α.
source: The promoters are conserved from frog to human and, along with alternative splicing, give rise to nine different transcript variants of HNF4α (Huang et al., 2009) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2009 and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The major isoforms of the P1 promoter are HNF4α1/α2.
source: The major isoforms of the P1 promoter are HNF4α1/α2 while the P2 promoter gives rise to HNF4α7/α8: distinct first exons result in an altered A/B domain which harbors the activation function 1 (AF-1) while the DNA and ligand binding domains are identical.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about HNF4α isoforms.

claim: The P2 promoter gives rise to HNF4α7/α8.
source: The major isoforms of the P1 promoter are HNF4α1/α2 while the P2 promoter gives rise to HNF4α7/α8: distinct first exons result in an altered A/B domain which harbors the activation function 1 (AF-1) while the DNA and ligand binding domains are identical.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about HNF4α isoforms.

claim: Distinct first exons in HNF4α isoforms result in an altered A/B domain which harbors the activation function 1 (AF-1).
source: The major isoforms of the P1 promoter are HNF4α1/α2 while the P2 promoter gives rise to HNF4α7/α8: distinct first exons result in an altered A/B domain which harbors the activation function 1 (AF-1) while the DNA and ligand binding domains are identical.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about nuclear receptor structure.

claim: The DNA and ligand binding domains are identical between P1- and P2-HNF4α isoforms.
source: The major isoforms of the P1 promoter are HNF4α1/α2 while the P2 promoter gives rise to HNF4α7/α8: distinct first exons result in an altered A/B domain which harbors the activation function 1 (AF-1) while the DNA and ligand binding domains are identical.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about HNF4α isoforms.

claim: The large and small intestine are the only adult tissues that express both P1- and P2-HNF4α.
source: The two promoters are expressed under unique temporal and spatial conditions, with the large and small intestine being the only adult tissues that express both P1- and P2-HNF4α (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nakhei et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Tanaka et al., 2006; Nakhei et al., 1998).

claim: A loss of P1- but not P2-HNF4α has been noted in colon cancer.
source: While a loss of P1- but not P2-HNF4α has been noted in colon cancer (Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006), the specific roles of the HNF4α isoforms remain obscure.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Chellappa et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2006).

claim: P1-driven HNF4α acts as a tumor suppressor in mouse liver.
source: For example, P1-driven HNF4α acts as a tumor suppressor in mouse liver (Hatziapostolou et al., 2011; Walesky et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Hatziapostolou et al., 2011; Walesky et al., 2013a).

claim: The HNF4A gene and protein are amplified in human colon cancer.
source: In contrast, the HNF4A gene and protein are amplified in human colon cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Zhang et al., 2014) although the different isoforms were not distinguished in those studies.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Zhang et al., 2014).

claim: Ectopic expression of P1- but not P2-HNF4α decreased the tumorigenic potential of the human colon cancer cell line HCT116 in a mouse xenograft model.
source: We recently showed that ectopic expression of P1- but not P2-HNF4α decreased the tumorigenic potential of the human colon cancer cell line HCT116 in a mouse xenograft model (Vuong et al., 2015), suggesting that the different HNF4α isoforms may indeed play distinct roles in the colon.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vuong et al., 2015.

claim: In wildtype mice, P1/P2 antibody shows HNF4α expression in both crypt and surface epithelial cells.
source: The P1/P2 antibody, which recognizes both P1- and P2-HNF4α, shows HNF4α expression in both crypt and surface epithelial cells (Figure 1B), as reported previously (Ahn et al., 2008; Darsigny et al., 2009; Chahar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Darsigny et al., 2009; Chahar et al., 2014).

claim: P1-HNF4α is expressed mainly in the differentiated compartment, not in the proliferative compartment as defined by NKCC1 staining.
source: In contrast, the isoform-specific antibodies reveal that P1-HNF4α is expressed mainly in the differentiated compartment, not in the proliferative compartment as defined by NKCC1 staining (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with immunofluorescence data.

claim: P2-HNF4α was observed primarily in the bottom half of the crypt.
source: P2-HNF4α was observed primarily in the bottom half of the crypt (Figure 1B) and co-localized with the proliferation marker Ki67 in isolated colonic crypts (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with immunofluorescence data.

claim: P2-HNF4α co-localized with the proliferation marker Ki67 in isolated colonic crypts.
source: P2-HNF4α was observed primarily in the bottom half of the crypt (Figure 1B) and co-localized with the proliferation marker Ki67 in isolated colonic crypts (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with immunofluorescence data.

claim: P2-HNF4α was notably absent from the surface epithelium.
source: While there was some expression of P2-HNF4α in the differentiated compartment (i.e., non Ki67 expressing cells), it was notably absent from the surface epithelium (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with immunofluorescence data.

claim: HNF4A expression is decreased in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients.
source: Previous studies showed that HNF4A expression is decreased in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients and intestine-specific deletion of the mouse Hnf4a gene increases susceptibility to dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis (Ahn et al., 2008) and can lead to chronic inflammation even in the absence of DSS (Darsigny et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Darsigny et al., 2009).

claim: Intestine-specific deletion of the mouse Hnf4a gene increases susceptibility to dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis.
source: Previous studies showed that HNF4A expression is decreased in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients and intestine-specific deletion of the mouse Hnf4a gene increases susceptibility to dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis (Ahn et al., 2008) and can lead to chronic inflammation even in the absence of DSS (Darsigny et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahn et al., 2008.

claim: Intestine-specific deletion of the mouse Hnf4a gene can lead to chronic inflammation even in the absence of DSS.
source: Previous studies showed that HNF4A expression is decreased in human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients and intestine-specific deletion of the mouse Hnf4a gene increases susceptibility to dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis (Ahn et al., 2008) and can lead to chronic inflammation even in the absence of DSS (Darsigny et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darsigny et al., 2009.

claim: There was a statistically significant decrease in total HNF4α following 5 days of DSS treatment in WT mice.
source: We treated young adult male mice (WT) with 2.5% DSS and found a statistically significant decrease in total HNF4α following 5 days of DSS treatment, as others have observed (Ahn et al., 2008; Chahar et al., 2014), and an increase in HNF4α during the recovery phase, especially P1-HNF4α (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A,B with immunoblot data and supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2008; Chahar et al., 2014).

claim: There was an increase in HNF4α during the recovery phase after DSS treatment, especially P1-HNF4α.
source: We treated young adult male mice (WT) with 2.5% DSS and found a statistically significant decrease in total HNF4α following 5 days of DSS treatment, as others have observed (Ahn et al., 2008; Chahar et al., 2014), and an increase in HNF4α during the recovery phase, especially P1-HNF4α (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A,B with immunoblot data.

claim: P1-HNF4α was also expressed near the bottom of the crypt after DSS treatment.
source: Contrary to the restricted expression of P1-HNF4α in the differentiated compartment in untreated mice, P1-HNF4α was also expressed near the bottom of the crypt after DSS treatment (Figure 2C), consistent with substantial loss of proliferating cells following DSS treatment (Tessner et al., 1998).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with immunofluorescence data and supported by citation to Tessner et al., 1998.

claim: P1-HNF4α is greatly reduced in tumors in the AOM+DSS mouse model of colitis-associated colon cancer compared to untreated controls.
source: In a mouse model of colitis-associated colon cancer (CAC) in which a single injection of azoxymethane (AOM) is followed by multiple treatments of DSS in the drinking water, we found that P1-HNF4α is greatly reduced in tumors compared to untreated controls but that total HNF4α protein was only marginally reduced (Figure 2D), suggesting that P2-HNF4α was not affected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with immunoblot data.

claim: Total HNF4α protein was only marginally reduced in tumors in the AOM+DSS mouse model.
source: In a mouse model of colitis-associated colon cancer (CAC) in which a single injection of azoxymethane (AOM) is followed by multiple treatments of DSS in the drinking water, we found that P1-HNF4α is greatly reduced in tumors compared to untreated controls but that total HNF4α protein was only marginally reduced (Figure 2D), suggesting that P2-HNF4α was not affected.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with immunoblot data.

claim: P2-HNF4α was not affected in tumors in the AOM+DSS mouse model.
source: In a mouse model of colitis-associated colon cancer (CAC) in which a single injection of azoxymethane (AOM) is followed by multiple treatments of DSS in the drinking water, we found that P1-HNF4α is greatly reduced in tumors compared to untreated controls but that total HNF4α protein was only marginally reduced (Figure 2D), suggesting that P2-HNF4α was not affected.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that total HNF4α was only marginally reduced while P1-HNF4α was greatly reduced, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The P1-HNF4α decrease in AOM+DSS tumors correlated with an increase in active Src (pSrc).
source: The P1-HNF4α decrease correlated with an increase in active Src (pSrc), consistent with our earlier finding that Src specifically phosphorylates and causes the degradation of human P1- but not P2-HNF4α (Chellappa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with immunoblot data and supported by citation to Chellappa et al., 2012.

claim: Src specifically phosphorylates and causes the degradation of human P1- but not P2-HNF4α.
source: The P1-HNF4α decrease correlated with an increase in active Src (pSrc), consistent with our earlier finding that Src specifically phosphorylates and causes the degradation of human P1- but not P2-HNF4α (Chellappa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chellappa et al., 2012.

claim: A specific loss of P1-HNF4α protein was observed in a mouse model of sporadic, non-colitis colon cancer.
source: We also observed a specific loss of P1-HNF4α protein in a mouse model of sporadic, non-colitis colon cancer (Figure 2E), as we observed previously in humans (Chellappa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with immunoblot data and supported by citation to Chellappa et al., 2012.

claim: The HNF4α protein level in the distal colon of the exon swap mice is equivalent to that of WT littermates.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that the HNF4α protein level in the distal colon of the exon swap mice is equivalent to that of WT littermates, and that P2-HNF4α is the major isoform in the distal colon (Figure 3A top right and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A top right and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E with immunoblot data.

claim: P2-HNF4α is the major isoform in the distal colon.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that the HNF4α protein level in the distal colon of the exon swap mice is equivalent to that of WT littermates, and that P2-HNF4α is the major isoform in the distal colon (Figure 3A top right and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A top right and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E with immunoblot data.

claim: In α1HMZ mice, P1-HNF4α was detected in all epithelial cells in both the bottom of the crypt and the surface epithelium.
source: In α1HMZ mice, P1-HNF4α was detected in all epithelial cells in both the bottom of the crypt and the surface epithelium; a similar ubiquitous expression was observed for P2-HNF4α in α7HMZ mice (Figure 3A bottom).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A bottom with immunofluorescence data.

claim: A ubiquitous expression was observed for P2-HNF4α in α7HMZ mice.
source: In α1HMZ mice, P1-HNF4α was detected in all epithelial cells in both the bottom of the crypt and the surface epithelium; a similar ubiquitous expression was observed for P2-HNF4α in α7HMZ mice (Figure 3A bottom).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A bottom with immunofluorescence data.

claim: After 53 days of AOM+DSS treatment, the α1HMZ mice had significantly fewer and smaller tumors compared to WT controls.
source: After 53 days of AOM+DSS treatment, the α1HMZ mice had significantly fewer and smaller tumors compared to WT controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with tumor count and size data.

claim: Despite similar crypt length in untreated WT and α1HMZ mice, the α1HMZ mice did not exhibit the characteristic increase in crypt length associated with mutagen exposure observed in WT mice.
source: In addition, despite similar crypt length in untreated WT and α1HMZ mice, the α1HMZ mice did not exhibit the characteristic increase in crypt length associated with mutagen exposure observed in WT mice (Richards, 1977) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C with crypt length measurements and supported by citation to Richards, 1977.

claim: The crypt length decreased in α1HMZ mice after AOM+DSS treatment compared to both treated WT and untreated α1HMZ.
source: In fact, the crypt length decreased compared to both treated WT and untreated α1HMZ.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C with crypt length measurements.

claim: Fewer infiltrating immune cells were observed in treated α1HMZ mice compared to WT.
source: We also observed fewer infiltrating immune cells (Figure 3C right) as well as decreased spleen-to-body weight ratio in the treated α1HMZ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C right with histological images.

claim: Decreased spleen-to-body weight ratio was observed in the treated α1HMZ mice.
source: We also observed fewer infiltrating immune cells (Figure 3C right) as well as decreased spleen-to-body weight ratio in the treated α1HMZ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A with spleen-to-body weight ratio data.

claim: After 85 days of AOM+DSS treatment, the difference in tumor number between α1HMZ and WT mice was less pronounced.
source: After 85 days of treatment, the difference in tumor number was less pronounced: a significant decrease in tumor number was observed in α1HMZ mice only in the smallest tumors (0–2 mm) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with tumor count data.

claim: A significant decrease in tumor number was observed in α1HMZ mice only in the smallest tumors (0–2 mm) after 85 days of AOM+DSS treatment.
source: After 85 days of treatment, the difference in tumor number was less pronounced: a significant decrease in tumor number was observed in α1HMZ mice only in the smallest tumors (0–2 mm) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with tumor count data stratified by size.

claim: The α7HMZ mice exhibited a greater tumor load and tumor number than their WT controls after 53–64 days of AOM+DSS treatment.
source: In contrast to α1HMZ mice, the α7HMZ mice exhibited a greater tumor load and tumor number than their WT controls after 53–64 days of treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E with tumor count and load data.

claim: At 85 days of AOM+DSS treatment, the increased tumor burden effect in α7HMZ mice was lost mainly due to increased tumor burden in the WT mice.
source: However, at the later time point (85 days), the effect was lost mainly due to increased tumor burden in the WT mice (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B with tumor data.

claim: There was no difference in the percent of Ki67-staining cells between WT and α7HMZ mice after 53–64 days of AOM+DSS treatment.
source: Interestingly, there was no difference in the percent of Ki67-staining cells between WT and α7HMZ mice (53–64 day treatment) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D with Ki67 staining quantification.

claim: There was a ~73% mortality rate for α7HMZ mice after DSS treatment that occurred starting after three days of recovery.
source: There was a ~73% mortality rate for α7HMZ mice that occurred starting after three days of recovery when the mice were switched to normal tap water (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with survival curve data.

claim: During the recovery phase after DSS treatment, α7HMZ mice exhibited a significant decrease in body weight compared to their WT littermates.
